title: Budge Budge, 1914
hookLine: the Komagata Maru's passengers returned to India and many were shot on arrival

lines: A SHIP HELD IN VANCOUVER HARBOR.
A SHORE THEY CAN SEE, NOT REACH.
BACK TO A LANDING NEAR CALCUTTA.
cards: A ship lies at anchor in Vancouver harbor. On board are passengers from Punjab, Sikh, Muslim and Hindu, who have paid to cross an ocean for work. Canada won't let them land.
For weeks they wait on deck, short of food and water, looking at a shore they can see and cannot reach. At last the ship is forced to turn around. Its name is the Komagata Maru.
The long voyage back ends at a riverside landing near Calcutta called Budge Budge, and the welcome there is worse than the one they left.

teach.b: A Sikh businessman, Gurdit Singh, had chartered the Komagata Maru to carry Punjabi migrants to Canada. Canadian rules were written to keep them out, and the passengers were refused. That's once.

teach.h: A TRAIN WAITING AT BUDGE BUDGE.
teach.b: When the ship reached Budge Budge in 1914, the British authorities, who suspected the passengers of ties to the Ghadar movement, wanted to put them straight onto a train for Punjab.
Accounts say the passengers wanted to go into Calcutta instead, and some set out walking, carrying the Guru Granth Sahib with them.
Police and troops confronted them, and there was firing. Passengers were killed, others wounded, others arrested. Gurdit Singh escaped and went into hiding.
Refused by Canada, they were now refused even the freedom to walk where they chose in their own country.
When Babur's armies fell on the towns of Punjab, Guru Nanak sang a hymn of protest, at Ang 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib.
In grief he asks the Creator: there was such slaughter, such crying out; did You feel no pain?

The Babarvani hymns don't explain suffering away. They name it, and bring it before God. Sikhs remember Budge Budge with a memorial at the landing, in that same spirit: not hiding the wound, naming it.

how: Sikhs remember the Komagata Maru and the Budge Budge shootings as part of their community's history; there are memorials at Budge Budge and in Vancouver, and the passengers are recalled in gurdwaras and community gatherings.

games.q: you've come home after weeks at sea. a train is waiting to take you straight to Punjab. what do some of the passengers do?
o: set out walking toward Calcutta, carrying the Guru Granth Sahib.
go back on board the ship.
games.why: accounts say some set out walking with the Guru Granth Sahib. police and troops confronted them, and there was firing.

practice: Think of people who have been refused somewhere, at a border, a door, a desk or a family table; you don't need their names.
Picture them standing just outside, close enough to see in, and keep them company in your thoughts as you breathe. If you pray, pray for them in your own way, or say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Budge Budge. The landing near Calcutta where the Komagata Maru's passengers came home, and where police fired on them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: turned away twice. Once at Vancouver harbor, and once more at the landing back home. Rest well.
